pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 9–11 — many ocean animals make remarkable migrations (humpback whales travel thousands of miles between feeding and breeding grounds; sea turtles return to their natal beach to nest), and these journeys are linked to seasonal food supplies and reproduction.
• Standards — UK (DfE Upper KS2): Y5/Y6 life cycles and habitats; builds on the general Animals-of-the-World migration concept toward marine specifics and geographic reasoning.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS1-1 (life-cycle stages) and 4-LS1-1/behaviour-for-survival; MS-LS1-4 (behaviours that support reproduction) — migration as a survival/reproduction behaviour.
• Operational details: three goals — (1) describe ONE migration in detail (humpback whale or sea turtle); (2) explain the DRIVERS: seasonal food availability (feed where/when plankton/krill bloom) and breeding needs (calve/nest in safe, often warmer or natal, sites); (3) grasp the SCALE (thousands of miles). Core reasoning: the journey is a timed response to a shifting resource — animals go where food is now, and return to breed where young are safest. Uses the five-oceans geography and food-web knowledge already built.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~9): describes one migration and says it's thousands of miles; Tier B (~10): names both drivers (food + breeding); Tier C (~11): explains WHY the timing/route follows seasonal food and safe breeding sites, reasoning from resource to route.
bestPractices: Anchor in ONE vivid, well-documented case studied in depth (humpback: polar feeding grounds ↔ tropical breeding waters; or turtle natal homing) rather than many shallow examples.
Make the two drivers explicit and separable: FEEDING migration (follow seasonal food blooms) vs BREEDING migration (reach safe/natal sites) — and show a single species doing both across the year.
Convey scale with maps and real distances/times (thousands of miles; months at sea) so 'remarkable' is quantified, not just adjectival.
Link to seasons and productivity: cold, nutrient-rich waters bloom in summer — that's why feeding grounds are polar and seasonal — tying migration to food-web/upwelling ideas.
Address navigation lightly (turtles/whales sense magnetic fields, cues) as wonder, while keeping the assessed core on WHY (food+breeding) and scale.
keyRepresentations: An annual migration map with route, distance and season markers (feeding ↔ breeding)
A seasonal-productivity overlay showing food blooms the animal follows
A split 'feeding ground vs breeding ground' comparison (cold/rich vs warm/safe)
A timeline linking months → location → activity (feed / travel / breed)
commonMisconceptions: 'Animals migrate just because it gets cold/they feel like it' — missing the specific food and breeding drivers.
'The journey is short / they wander randomly' — underestimating the thousands-of-miles scale and the directed, repeated route.
'They feed and breed in the same place' — not grasping the separation that necessitates the journey.
'Migration is effortless' — ignoring the energetic cost and risk that make the food/breeding payoff worth it.
Confusing migration (round-trip, repeated, purposeful) with one-way dispersal or getting lost.

learn.summary: For ages 9–11: ocean animals such as humpback whales and sea turtles make remarkable migrations (thousands of miles) driven by two separable factors — following seasonal food supply and reaching safe breeding/nesting sites. Learners should describe one migration in detail, name both drivers, grasp the scale, and reason from shifting resources to the route and its timing. Core insight: the journey is a timed response to a resource that appears and vanishes with the seasons, combined with a need to breed where young are safest.

activities.title: Migrate through the year with a humpback whale
feedback: If a learner lingers in polar water too long, point to the fading bloom and the due calf: 'Food is running out here and the calf needs warm, safe water — what is lost by staying?'
If a learner treats warm water as 'just nicer', ask what the whale GAINS at the warm end beyond comfort (a safe place to give birth) and at the cold end (abundant food).
Reinforce scale: 'The meter has passed a thousand miles and you are still travelling — this round trip runs to thousands of miles.'

If timing is ignored, highlight likely seasonal cues (shortening days, cooling water, food dropping off) that are thought to signal when to leave each year (scientists are still studying exactly which cues matter most), and note this is an instinctive cycle rather than a planned decision.
activities.rationale: Advancing time and watching food and route change together is intended to make the food and breeding drivers and the scale concrete rather than merely stated. This is a research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
learnerActions: Start in cold polar seas and advance the seasons step by step (for example with a season dial or by moving through labelled months).
Watch a productivity/food layer bloom in polar summer — feed and fatten the whale while krill are abundant.
As autumn arrives and the bloom fades, decide what to do: staying means little food while a calf is due; set off and travel thousands of miles to warm tropical breeding grounds to calve, then return.
Track the distance travelled on a distance or energy meter and note how mistiming the departure (lingering too long) costs the whale energy and risks the calf.
Optionally switch to a sea-turtle mode that adds returning to nest on the same beach or stretch of coast where the turtle hatched.
State in your own words why the whale leaves rich feeding water for food-poor tropics, and name each leg's driver.
activities.intendedInsight: The migration is not restlessness or seeking comfort — it is chasing food that appears and disappears with the seasons AND reaching a safe place to breed, a round trip forced because food and safe breeding sites are not in the same place at the same time.

activities.title: Explore a migration atlas (descriptive case study)
feedback: If a learner thinks any water would do, point to the productivity overlay and the fixed breeding/natal site: specific places matter.
Prompt estimation before revealing the total: 'How far do you think — hundreds or thousands of miles?' then compare to the real figure.
activities.rationale: A tappable atlas presents the case, drivers and scale clearly and supports the descriptive goals; because it is static it cannot let the learner move with the shifting food, so it is intended to be paired with the timed activity. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
learnerActions: Open a route map of one species' annual migration with tappable waypoints: feeding ground, open-ocean transit, breeding ground.
At each waypoint, read the season, what the animal is doing (feed / travel / breed), and the cumulative distance travelled.
Toggle a seasonal-productivity overlay to see where and when food blooms along the route.
Describe the migration in detail from start to finish, including both drivers and the total distance.
activities.intendedInsight: A single species feeds in one place and breeds in another at different times of year, and the specific destinations (particular feeding grounds, a natal beach) matter — the route is directed and repeated, not random wandering or one-way dispersal.

activities.title: Order the year and estimate the scale (check understanding)
feedback: If a learner labels both legs with the same single reason, split the trip: cold end = food, warm end = breeding/calving.
If scale is underestimated, confirm the real distance (thousands of miles) and note this is among the longest migrations of any mammal.
If timing is left to 'the whale decides', introduce reliable annual cues — day length, temperature, food dropping off.

For the year-round-food case: in this model, fading food would no longer be a reason to leave the polar seas, but a whale due to calve would still need to travel to safe warm tropical waters to give birth — and because the tropics have little food, it would still need to come back to the polar feeding grounds afterwards. So food alone does not explain the whole journey.
activities.rationale: A sequencing step, driver questions, a scale estimate and a transfer case faithfully check all three evidence goals plus the reasoning behind them. Recognition and ordering tasks check understanding but do not by themselves elicit extended independent explanation, so the activity also asks the learner to state the reasoning in their own words. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
learnerActions: Put the annual migration stages in order (feed in polar summer → travel → breed in tropics → return).
Choose between food and breeding as the driver for each leg of the trip.
Estimate the total distance of the migration (slider or multiple choice) and compare to the real figure.
Consider a 'what if': if the polar seas stayed rich in food all year, would the whale still make the trip, and which leg would it still need?
Explain in one or two sentences WHY the timing of departure follows the seasons.
activities.intendedInsight: Both drivers and the scale can be stated independently, and the timing of the journey is tied to seasonal change rather than whim; in this model, even with year-round polar food, a whale due to calve would still need to travel to safe warm waters to give birth, so food alone does not explain the journey.

activities.title: Hear from a scientist who tracks tagged animals (wonder supplement)
feedback: Treat navigation lightly as wonder; redirect the assessed reasoning to the two drivers and the scale.
If the learner attributes the journey to the animal 'planning like a person', reframe it as a seasonally-cued instinctive cycle that recurs at the same time each year.
activities.rationale: A tagging scientist's account is engaging and can field navigation questions, but the drivers-and-scale reasoning is intended to be carried mainly by the map/timed activities; this serves as an optional supplement. Research-informed proposal, not a tested intervention.
learnerActions: Listen to or read a marine biologist recounting one tracked humpback's or turtle's year — where it went and when.
Ask or consider the question 'How do they find their way?' and discuss cues such as sensing magnetic fields.
Keep a note of what the animal was doing at each stage to connect the story back to the food and breeding drivers.
activities.intendedInsight: Navigation and tracking add wonder and a human perspective, while the core reasoning stays on why (food + breeding) and how far.

constraints: Anchor in ONE vivid, well-documented case studied in depth (humpback: polar feeding ↔ tropical breeding; or turtle natal homing) rather than many shallow examples.

Keep the two drivers explicit and separable — feeding migration (follow seasonal food blooms) versus breeding migration (reach safe/natal sites) — and show a single species doing both across the year.
Quantify 'remarkable' with real distances and times (thousands of miles; months at sea) using maps, not just adjectives.
Link feeding grounds to seasonal productivity: cold, nutrient-rich waters bloom in summer, tying migration to food-web and upwelling ideas already built.
Address navigation only lightly (magnetic-field sensing, cues) as wonder; keep the assessed core on why (food + breeding) and scale.

Recognition and ordering tasks check understanding but do not by themselves require the learner to construct an extended explanation; include at least one task where the learner states the reasoning in their own words.
A static atlas or a dialogue can present the case and drivers; neither is uniquely necessary, and each is paired with an activity that lets timing and food change together.
A globe or 3D view can show the route wrapping the planet; the 2D seasonal map already carries the causal mechanism, so richer media are optional rather than required.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the two NOAA sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source claims were removed from activity sourceClaims arrays because each rationale states a pedagogical-efficacy point, which the NOAA sources (migration facts) do not directly support; the facts themselves remain within the activity text.

The original 3D-interactive entry asserted '3D adds cost without deepening the driver insight'; this has been softened to a scoped observation that the 2D map already carries the mechanism, without claiming 3D adds nothing in general.

The original rationale implied the timed simulation is the only way to make drivers 'felt' and that the atlas 'can't let the driver click'; retained as scoped affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

Departure timing is cued by seasonal signals (day length, temperature, declining food) and is instinctive, not a conscious plan — learner-facing text avoids implying animal deliberation; the simulation's 'decide' framing is explicitly reframed as instinctive in feedback.

Distance claims ('thousands of miles', 'among the longest migrations of any mammal') are carried from unverified sources; presented as the given figures and used for comparison rather than asserted as verified.

A prior draft stated the humpback trip was 'among the longest animal migrations'; corrected to 'of any mammal' to match the source and avoid a factual overstatement (some non-mammal migrations are longer).

The 'migration is effortless' and 'one-way dispersal/getting lost' misconceptions are addressed via the distance/energy meter and mistiming penalty, and via the 'directed and repeated, not random' framing; they could be made more explicit if desired.

probeDeeper: The whale leaves cold water FULL of food to go where there's hardly any. If comfort were the reason, why give up the food? What must it be getting instead?
What could tell an animal, without a calendar, that it's the right week to leave every year?
A turtle swims across an ocean to lay eggs on the exact beach where it hatched. What does that tell you about whether migration is about comfort?
If the polar seas stayed rich in food all year round, would the whale still make the trip? Which leg might it still need?
assess.correctAnswer: Comfort isn't the driver. Marine migrations are tied to food and breeding on a seasonal cycle: whales feed in cold, nutrient-rich polar waters in summer where food is abundant, then travel to warm tropical waters to breed and give birth where calves are safer, even though there's little food there. The timing is cued by the seasons (changing day length, temperature, food supply), not by a whim. Sea turtles show the reproduction side too — they return to the very beach where they hatched to lay their eggs.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Animals migrate to be comfortable / escape the cold' — attributes the journey to preference or feelings.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Split the trip: cold end = food, warm end = breeding/calving. Ask what the whale GAINS at each end beyond comfort.
errorPatterns.distractor: It just prefers warm water — it goes on holiday to the tropics to get away from the cold.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains migration as seeking nicer weather; can't say why an animal would leave rich feeding grounds for food-poor tropics.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Animals decide/plan to migrate' — treats it as a conscious choice rather than a seasonally-cued instinctive cycle.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Introduce cues — day length, temperature, food dropping off — that reliably trigger departure each year, the same time annually.
errorPatterns.distractor: The whale decides it's time for a change and plans the trip like a person planning a holiday.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the animal 'chooses' to go; no mention of seasonal or environmental cues triggering it.

errorPatterns.pattern: Underestimates the scale / thinks any water is as good as any other — misses that specific destinations matter (natal beach, particular feeding grounds).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Map a real humpback or turtle route; highlight fidelity to a specific natal beach and the true distance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Guesses short distances, or says a turtle could nest on any beach; surprised by 'thousands of miles' and 'same beach it hatched on'.

responseLevels.gap: Explains migration by comfort/preference; can't account for the round trip or the timing.
responseLevels.full: Assigns each leg its driver (polar feeding vs tropical breeding), grounds the timing in seasonal cues, cites scale and site-fidelity (natal beach), and reasons about a new case such as year-round food.
responseLevels.partial: Knows migration links to food and breeding and can quote the scale, but treats the two ends as one vague reason, or leaves the timing/cues unexplained.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A humpback whale swims thousands of miles from cold polar seas to warm tropical waters and back every year. A child says 'it goes to the warm place because it doesn't like being cold — like us wanting a holiday in the sun'. Do you think staying comfortable is the real reason? What actually drives a journey that long, and how would the whale know when to set off?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child with the 'comfort/holiday' idea gives feelings as the cause and can't explain the round trip (why leave good feeding to go somewhere with little food); a child with the concept ties each leg to food OR breeding and grounds the timing in the seasons. Asking 'how would it know when to set off' exposes whether they have a seasonal cue or just a preference.

sources.claim: Humpback whales migrate thousands of miles between cold, productive high-latitude feeding grounds (summer) and warmer low-latitude breeding/calving grounds (winter) — among the longest migrations of any mammal.
sources.source: NOAA Fisheries — Humpback whale species profile

sources.claim: Many sea turtles perform natal homing — returning to nest on or near the beach where they hatched — after long ocean migrations, linking migration to reproduction.
sources.source: NOAA Fisheries — Sea turtles / natal homing
